candidate.answerReason: A nonzero translation by one complete repeat and a half-turn about a suitable point on \(\ell\) preserve the pattern. Each listed reflection reverses the direction of the diagonal attachments, so neither reflection preserves it. Exactly two kinds qualify.

methods.label: Check each kind of motion
methods.explanation:
We are counting kinds of motion, so one working nonidentity example is enough to qualify a kind.

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_10A_Q08_question_fig1.svg)

A translation parallel to \(\ell\) works: slide the figure from one upper square to the next upper square. This is a nonzero translation by one full repeat, so every square and attached segment lands on an identical part of the infinite pattern.

A rotation also works. Take an upper square and the neighboring lower square to its right. The midpoint of the segment joining their centers lies on \(\ell\), because the equal squares extend equally far above and below the line. A \(180^\circ\) rotation about this midpoint exchanges the upper and lower squares throughout the pattern. Each upper right diagonal attachment becomes a lower left attachment, and conversely. The line \(\ell\) also maps onto itself.

Neither listed reflection works. Every short diagonal attachment rises from left to right. Reflection across \(\ell\), or across any line perpendicular to \(\ell\), makes these diagonals fall from left to right. The original pattern has no attachments in that direction.

Thus rotation and translation qualify, while both reflection kinds fail. The answer is \(\boxed{2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
